documents.title: Generative AI (guidance incl. 'Adhere to the Academic Policy')
documents.summary: An IT-office guidance page that welcomes thoughtful GenAI use and lists safe-use practices (verify output, protect confidential data, check with OIT before buying tools, watch for phishing). On academic use it sets no rule: it points to College and School policies and tells faculty to state acceptable use in class.
documents.stance_why: The page says "Georgia Tech encourages the thoughtful use of Gen AI technologies", but for classes it only says to "Examine the handbooks and policies of your respective College and School" and that faculty "communicate explicitly to their students about the acceptable use of Generative AI". It sets no course-level rule itself and hands the decision to Schools and instructors, so delegates.

units.why: Sets an institution-level welcoming position: Georgia Tech "encourages the thoughtful use" of GenAI. This is a default of permitting/encouraging use (P02), addressed to the whole community and general in phase; 'encourages' maps to should.
units.anchor: Georgia Tech encourages the thoughtful use of Gen AI technologies

units.why: Lists the principles that frame all GenAI use: "safeguarding information security and data privacy, adhering to legal and regulatory standards, respecting copyright laws, and maintaining academic honesty and integrity." A preamble of principles fits P56, not the narrower privacy or copyright types, which are coded separately below.
units.anchor: safeguarding information security and data privacy, adhering to legal and regulatory standards, respecting copyright laws
units.frag_start: Key aspects to consider while leveraging
units.policy: Key aspects of using Gen AI tools are safeguarding information security and data privacy, adhering to legal and regulatory standards, respecting copyright laws, and maintaining academic honesty and integrity.

units.why: Defines GenAI as "a category of AI capable of analyzing and emulating datasets to generate various forms of content", which sets what the guidance covers. A definition is informs and belongs under P61.
units.anchor: a category of AI capable of analyzing and emulating datasets to generate various forms
units.frag_start: Generative AI, or GenAI for short
units.frag_end: videos, and code in response to given inputs or instructions

units.why: Tells readers to "Examine the handbooks and policies of your respective College and School" for academic rules; the university page itself sets no rule and defers to lower units. That is the decision being placed with Colleges and Schools (P04), not a fallback rule, addressed to all readers.
units.anchor: Examine the handbooks and policies of your respective College and School
units.frag_end: particularly those pertaining to students and faculty

units.why: States that "Schools will revise and formulate new policies" as understanding of GenAI impacts grows. This is a statement that policy is provisional and will change (P54), by admin units, so informs.
units.anchor: Schools will revise and formulate new policies

units.why: "Faculty members should, in the interim, communicate explicitly to their students about the acceptable use of Generative AI" tells instructors to state AI expectations to students. That is the communicate-expectations type (P09), instructor actor, course-start, should.
units.anchor: Faculty members should, in the interim, communicate explicitly to their students about the acceptable use
units.frag_start: Faculty members should, in the interim

units.why: "Students should also proactively seek clarification from their instructors" about AI policies when unsure; this is the ask-first type (P10), student actor, should.
units.anchor: Students should also proactively seek clarification from their instructors regarding these policies

units.why: Warns that GenAI makes phishing emails and "deepfakes" easier and tells readers to follow security practices and report suspicious messages. It is a harm of AI named with a safeguard; it is not about data privacy (P50) or learning, so the nearest type is P53 (harms).
units.anchor: adhere to security best practices and to report any dubious messages
units.frag_start: The advent of Generative AI has
units.policy: Generative AI makes it easier to craft advanced phishing emails and deepfakes; adhere to security best practices and report any dubious messages to phishing@gatech.edu.

units.why: States that AI-created content "can sometimes be incorrect, deceptive, or entirely made up"; the point is that output must be checked before publishing, which is P31.
units.anchor: Content created by AI can sometimes be incorrect, deceptive, or entirely made up

units.why: Notes AI output "might also include material that is protected by copyright". Copyright concern about AI output fits P52, informs.
units.anchor: it might also include material that is protected by copyright

units.why: "you bear responsibility for that content" makes the publisher accountable for AI-generated material they publish. Responsibility for submitted/published content is P29 (not P31, which is about verification).
units.anchor: you bear responsibility for that content

units.why: "You should not input data categorized as PII ... into publicly accessible Generative AI tools" forbids entering sensitive data into public tools. It is about personal and confidential data, so P50 rather than P49 (course materials).
units.anchor: You should not input data categorized as PII

units.why: Data of "Level 2 or higher in confidentiality should only be used with Generative AI tools that have undergone evaluation and received approval"; this prefers vetted tools for confidential data (P50).
units.anchor: should only be used with Generative AI tools that have undergone evaluation and received approval
units.policy: Data that is considered Level 2 or higher in confidentiality should only be used with Generative AI tools that have undergone evaluation and received approval from Georgia Tech's Information Security and Data Privacy office.

units.why: Explains that "Information disclosed to Generative AI tools under standard settings is not confidential"; a fact giving the reason for the data rule, so P50 informs.
units.anchor: Information disclosed to Generative AI tools under standard settings is not confidential

units.why: Says OIT "is actively working to ensure that any tools acquired ... are equipped with suitable privacy and security measures" and is exploring its own GenAI service offerings. This describes institutional provision of a sanctioned tool (P17), informs, admin actor.
units.anchor: As OIT explores introducing its own Gen AI service offerings

units.why: Requires that "vendor-supplied generative AI tools" "undergo a risk evaluation by OIT before they are put to use" and asks people to contact OIT before purchasing. This is institutional review of AI vendors (P65), must.
units.anchor: It is imperative for vendor-supplied generative AI tools to undergo a risk evaluation by OIT
units.frag_end: before they are put to use
units.policy: Vendor-supplied generative AI tools must undergo a risk evaluation by OIT before they are put to use; contact OIT before purchasing any generative AI tools.

documents.title: Establishing Course Policies (Student Use of Artificial Intelligence section)
documents.summary: Teaching-center guidance telling instructors to put a GenAI policy in the syllabus and listing questions to settle (collaboration, level of use by assignment, documentation, citation). It prescribes no particular rule and points to example statements and a fuller policy document.
documents.stance_why: The section tells instructors to "Let your students know your expectations" and poses questions such as "Will the level of GenAI usage be the same for the entire course or will it differ by assignment?" It leaves every substantive choice to the instructor and sets no allow or ban itself, so delegates.

units.why: "Let your students know your expectations for how they should collaborate with and cite their use of Generative AI" tells instructors to communicate AI expectations in the syllabus. P09 (syllabus statement), instructor, course-start, should.
units.anchor: Let your students know your expectations for how they should collaborate with and cite

units.why: "Without including this information in your syllabus, students will not know how they can ethically use GenAI in your course." It is the stated reason for putting the AI statement in the syllabus, so P09 with informs.
units.anchor: Without including this information in your syllabus, students will not know how

units.why: Warns students may "resist using basic GenAI functions such as spelling and grammar assistants due to fear of penalization" if the syllabus is silent. It addresses writing-assistance tools, which are prose rules (P18), and tells instructors to clarify them; informs.
units.anchor: basic GenAI functions such as spelling and grammar assistants due to fear of penalization

units.why: Advises instructors to "consider students' engagement with GenAI as an extension of your collaboration and academic honesty policies". That treats AI like a collaborator under existing rules (P45), should.
units.anchor: consider students’ engagement with GenAI as an extension of your collaboration and academic honesty policies

units.why: Points instructors to a "curated document of cross-institutional examples of syllabus statements" and an "adaptable" policy document with statements; this is support for faculty drafting AI policy (P63).
units.anchor: explore this curated document of cross-institutional
units.policy: To get started creating a GenAI usage policy, explore the curated document of cross-institutional examples of syllabus statements on GenAI use, and the full AI policy document with adaptable GenAI syllabus statements.

units.why: The question "Under what circumstances is collaboration (whether with peers or GenAI) acceptable or even encouraged" leaves to each instructor when AI collaboration is allowed; it is a decision per instructor (P04), phrased as a prompt so should.
units.anchor: Under what circumstances is collaboration (whether with peers or GenAI) acceptable or even encouraged
units.policy: Instructors decide under what circumstances collaboration, with peers or GenAI, is acceptable or even encouraged (e.g. brainstorming, draft review, outline creation).

units.why: "Will you be incorporating GenAI usage into your assignments?" asks the instructor to decide on building AI into assignments; assignment redesign around AI is P35.
units.anchor: Will you be incorporating GenAI usage into your assignments?
units.policy: Instructors consider whether they will incorporate GenAI usage into their assignments.

units.why: "Will the level of GenAI usage be the same for the entire course or will it differ by assignment?" leaves to the instructor whether the rule varies per assignment, which is P04 (per assignment).
units.anchor: Will the level of GenAI usage be the same for the entire course
units.policy: Instructors decide whether the level of GenAI usage is the same for the entire course or differs by assignment.

units.why: Asks "How should students document their process of engagement with GenAI?" with options such as prompts, output, or a reflection on editing. This is keeping and submitting prompts/outputs/reflections (P26).
units.anchor: How should students document their process of engagement with GenAI?
units.policy: Instructors decide how students should document their process of engagement with GenAI, for example by showing prompts and/or the GenAI output, or writing a reflection on how they edited and refined the initial output.

units.why: "How do you expect the GenAI applications to show up in citations (e.g. APA, Chicago, MLA, etc.)?" asks instructors to set a citation expectation for AI use; disclosure/citation with each submission is P24 (no detail like prompt required, so not P25).
units.anchor: How do you expect the GenAI applications to show up in citations
units.policy: Instructors decide how GenAI applications are expected to show up in citations (e.g. APA, Chicago, MLA).

notes: Only the two included university-layer documents were coded; the ten course syllabi are screened deferred and were skipped. The CTL page's references to a full AI policy document with adaptable statements point to inaccessible files, so those statements were not coded. The CTL AI section is mostly question prompts to instructors; the units are coded as instructor-addressed 'should' guidance.
